p5-elf-b5-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Valk expected the long motorway hauls to be where the cold chain failed, but they were not. Valk’s loggers showed steady temperatures on the road and damaging spikes during the brief handovers at the loading docks. C says this. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what Valk’s loggers showed about where the cold chain broke down. “According to the text” means that the answer must be stated there. The cold chain is the series of steps that keeps chilled goods cold, and a logger is a small device that records the temperature.

steps.title: Find the result
steps.text: Valk “assumed the long motorway hauls would be where the cold chain failed. They were not.” The loggers showed that “the reefer units held their set point steadily for hour after hour on the road; the sharp, damaging spikes came instead during the brief handovers”.

steps.title: Explain the words
steps.text: The reefer units are the lorries’ cooling units, and the set point is the temperature they are set to keep. Spikes are sudden, short rises in temperature. The handovers were the moments “when pallets stood on unheated — but far from cold — loading docks while paperwork was checked and rear doors hung open”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C keeps both halves in the right places: steady on the road, spikes at the docks. A puts the failure on the motorway, which is what Valk expected but did not find. B moves the open doors from the docks to the motorway. D turns one operator’s winter into every operator in the region all year.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The temperature held on the road and spiked during the handovers at the docks. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: A matches what Valk expected at the start: that the long motorway hauls “would be where the cold chain failed”.
distractors.why_wrong: The text answers that expectation at once: “They were not.” On the road the reefer units “held their set point steadily for hour after hour” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The open rear doors really are in the text, and open doors would let warm air in.
distractors.why_wrong: The doors hung open during the brief handovers at the loading docks, while paperwork was checked (step 3). On the motorway the units held their set point, so B moves a real detail to the wrong part of the journey.

distractors.why_tempting: D sounds like a bold headline version of the finding, and the docks were indeed where the spikes came.
distractors.why_wrong: Valk is cautious about “how far the finding travels”: “We measured one operator, over one winter.” The text says nothing about every operator, the whole region or the whole year, and it never says how many deliveries were ruined.

p5-elf-b5-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “According to the text” questions, find the sentence that reports the result and check each part of an option against it. Here the result has two halves – steady on the road, spikes at the docks – and the right option must keep both in the right place.
p5-elf-b5-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Do not pick the option that matches the researcher’s first expectation. The text reports what Valk assumed and then says “They were not.”

p5-elf-b5-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text says that the sensor changed “not the scoreboard but the room”: bouts ran on without argument, crowds settled faster and matches finished on time, while very few decisions were reversed. So the main effect was on the conduct and pace of matches. That is B. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Imply” means that the answer is not stated word for word. Read what the text says about the sensor’s effects and work out which one it treats as the main effect.

steps.title: Find the small effect
steps.text: The officials expected “a flood of overturned decisions”, but “The flood never came.” Over a full season the sensor “reversed barely one call in thirty”. “Barely” marks this as a small change.

steps.title: Find the main change
steps.text: Then comes the key sentence: “What the system changed was not the scoreboard but the room.” The scoreboard stands for the results; the room stands for what happens around the fencing. A bout is a single fight, and a bout that stalled stopped for a while. The text lists the changes: “Bouts that once stalled while fencers protested now ran on without argument”, and “crowds settled faster, and matches finished on time.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B names the room, not the scoreboard: the conduct and pace of matches. A gives the small effect as if it were the main one, C turns the judges’ good record upside down, and D makes a forecast about other sports that the text never makes.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The sensor changed the conduct and pace of matches far more than the decisions. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: A uses the text’s own figure, one call in thirty, so it looks safely accurate.
distractors.why_wrong: The figure is true, but the text presents it as the small effect: the expected flood of overturned decisions never came (step 2). The main change, the text says, was “not the scoreboard but the room” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: C reuses the text’s words about the fast exchanges, and a machine is often brought in because people make mistakes.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite: the human judges “had been reading the fast exchanges better than anyone had credited”, and the sensor reversed barely one call in thirty (step 2). So it found very few of their calls wrong.

distractors.why_tempting: Machines replacing people is a familiar story, and the sensor was brought in “to replace its judges' eyes”.
distractors.why_wrong: The text is about one sport, tavro, and says nothing about other sports or the future. Aru even doubts that the change was a clean gain: “I am not certain quiet is the same thing as fairness.”

p5-elf-b5-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “imply” questions, look for a sentence that names the real change – here “not the scoreboard but the room” – and choose the option that restates it in plain words. A true detail that the text treats as minor is not the main effect.
p5-elf-b5-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: A precise number can feel like the safe choice. But the one-in-thirty figure is the effect the text plays down with “barely”, not the one it stresses.

p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text follows a pilot that tested the promise that tidal power runs on a timetable. On that narrow measure the pilot delivered, but the cost of servicing the turbines grew into “the line that decided whether the whole project made sense”. B covers both halves. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text. The right answer must cover the main line of the argument, not one fact or one person’s view.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: The first paragraph sets out the promise: the tide runs “on a schedule an engineer can print a year in advance”. The second reports that, on that narrow measure, the pilot kept it. The third turns to the trouble of reaching the machines, the fourth gives Toft’s and an economist’s views on cost, and the fifth gives the writer’s verdict.

steps.title: Find the verdict
steps.text: The writer concludes that “a resource you can predict is not yet a resource you can afford”. The tide behaved as promised, while the costs of servicing grew into “the line that decided whether the whole project made sense”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B names both halves: the tide’s predictability confirmed, and the cost of servicing as the deciding obstacle. A says the turbines failed and were shut down, C gives only the first paragraph’s fact, and D turns praise for predictability into a policy the text never proposes.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The pilot confirmed the tide’s timetable but found the cost of servicing to be the real obstacle. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The third paragraph dwells on problems: weed and barnacles on the blades, and a seal that “could not be reached for weeks”.
distractors.why_wrong: The turbines worked: the array fed power “on a schedule no wind farm could match”, and “The islands still draw their power from the Race.” The trouble was the cost of reaching them, not that they could not work (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: C is true: the first paragraph says that the tide runs on a schedule that can be printed a year ahead.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the starting point, not the point of the text. The text treats predictability as the settled half and moves on to the harder question of cost, which C leaves out (steps 2–3).

distractors.why_tempting: The first paragraph contrasts the tide with wind, which “arrives when it pleases”, and sunlight, which “quits at dusk”.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that tidal power should replace wind or solar. Its verdict is that a predictable resource “is not yet a resource you can afford” (step 3), which works against such a recommendation.

p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “mainly about” questions, map the text paragraph by paragraph and find the turn – here “However, the tide was never the difficult part.” The right option covers what comes before the turn and what comes after it.
p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: A true fact from the opening, such as the year-ahead timetable, can look like a summary. Check whether the option also includes the turn that the rest of the text is built on.

p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The second paragraph says that through its first three years the array “fed power to the islands on a schedule no wind farm could match”. C says the same. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the array achieved in its first three years. The array is the group of three turbines that the consortium lowered onto the bed of the Race. “According to the text” means that the answer must be stated there, so find the sentence about those years in the second paragraph.

steps.title: Find the sentence
steps.text: “Through its first three years the array fed power to the islands on a schedule no wind farm could match — you could look at a calendar and say, with fair confidence, when the turbines would be spinning hardest.”

steps.title: Note the limit
steps.text: The next sentence adds a limit: “In its strongest months the array ran close to the output its designers had modelled.” The text makes this claim only for the strongest months, not for every month.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C restates the predictable schedule. A stretches the strongest months to every month, B claims that the array met all the islands’ needs, which the text never says, and D reverses what happened to the maintenance costs.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The array delivered power on a schedule that could be predicted. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does say that the array ran “close to the output its designers had modelled”.
distractors.why_wrong: The text makes that claim only for “its strongest months” (step 3). A turns it into “every single month across the whole of the three years”, which the text never claims.

distractors.why_tempting: A working array wired to the island grid can sound like the islands’ whole power supply.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says that the array “fed power to the islands” on schedule (step 2), and at the end that the islands “still draw their power from the Race”. But it never says how much of their electricity the array supplied in its first three years, and it never mentions any other source of power that the array replaced.

distractors.why_tempting: The text talks about maintenance costs, so an option about them sounds connected.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite: the costs once filed under maintenance “swelled into the line that decided whether the whole project made sense”. They grew; nothing in the text says they fell.

p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: For “According to the text” questions about a result, find the sentence that reports it, then read the next sentence for limits. Here the predictable schedule is stated outright, and “In its strongest months” limits the claim about output.
p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Watch for an option that turns a limited claim into an absolute one. “In its strongest months” is not “every single month”.

p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The third paragraph says that the turbines could be serviced only in the brief calm of slack water, and only if the weather at the surface allowed, and that “Every retrieval meant a specialised vessel, a narrow tidal window, and a crew paid to wait for both.” A says this. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what made the turbines expensive to run, as the text explains it. The cost problem is described in the third paragraph, which begins: “However, the tide was never the difficult part.”

steps.title: Find the difficulty
steps.text: “The difficulty lay in reaching the machines.” A turbine on the floor of the channel “can be serviced only in the brief, calm minutes of slack water, and only then if the weather at the surface happens to cooperate.”

steps.title: Explain slack water
steps.text: Slack water, as the note under the text explains, is the short interval when a tidal current briefly stops running. So the time for repairs was short, and bad weather could take it away.

steps.title: Find the cost
steps.text: “Every retrieval meant a specialised vessel, a narrow tidal window, and a crew paid to wait for both.” A retrieval is a trip out to reach a turbine and bring it up, and a vessel is a ship or boat. These costs grew into “the line that decided whether the whole project made sense”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A gives exactly this problem of access. B invents early wear and replacement, C blames the tide, which behaved as forecast, and D names a cost the text never mentions.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The turbines could be serviced only in short windows that depended on the weather, which made every trip costly. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does mention trouble with the machines: barnacles and weed on the blades, and a seal that failed.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that the turbines wore out fast or had to be replaced early. The problem it names is reaching them for servicing (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The tide is the main subject of the text, so it can seem the natural place to look for the problem.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite: “the tide was never the difficult part”, and nobody who watched the array doubts that the current “will keep its appointments”. The difficulty lay in reaching the machines (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The turbines were wired to the island grid, so cabling is part of the project.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions the cost of cabling. The expense it names is servicing: the vessel, the narrow window and the crew paid to wait (step 4).

p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a question asks what the text says caused a problem, find the sentence that names it – here “The difficulty lay in reaching the machines.” – and match the option to that cause, not to other problems mentioned nearby.
p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Real details nearby, such as the barnacles, the failed seal and the grid connection, can lead you to a cause the text does not give. Keep to the cause the text itself names.

p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: Toft says that the pilot showed the current is “bankable” – a delivery schedule can be promised and kept – but not that the turbines can be serviced cheaply, and that “Those are not the same result”. So a resource can be reliable while the project built on it is too costly. That is D. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Imply” means that the answer is not stated word for word. The question is about Toft’s distinction: what follows from keeping a “bankable” current and servicing “the thing cheaply” apart?

steps.title: Find the two halves
steps.text: Toft says: “We showed the current is bankable — that you can promise a utility a delivery schedule and keep it.” Then: “What we did not show is that you can service the thing cheaply.” “Bankable” means reliable enough to count on, like money in the bank, and a utility is a company that supplies electricity.

steps.title: Find the gap between them
steps.text: Toft adds: “Those are not the same result, and people keep hearing the first when I say the second.” A reliable current and cheap servicing are two different things, and having the first does not give you the second.

steps.title: Draw the inference
steps.text: So a tidal resource can be reliable and predictable while the project built on it is still too costly to run. The economist makes the same point: “the tide is free, but the boat is not”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D states the gap between the two. A repeats only the first half of the distinction, and B and C both predict lower costs, which the text never does.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Being reliable does not by itself make a tidal project affordable. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: A is true to the text: Toft does say that the current is bankable and that a delivery schedule can be promised and kept.
distractors.why_wrong: A repeats only the first half of what Toft said (step 2). The question asks what the distinction implies, and the point of the distinction is that reliable is not the same as cheap to service (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The text praises the tide’s predictability over wind, so it can seem to follow that tidal power will end up cheaper too.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never compares the cost of tidal power with that of wind. Its point is that predictability does not make a project cheap (step 3), which works against B’s forecast.

distractors.why_tempting: Costs often fall as a new technology matures, so C sounds like a reasonable hope.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in the text says that servicing costs will fall. The economist’s point is that “the tide is free, but the boat is not” (step 4), and the writer measures the gap in “the price of every trip out to scrape a blade”.

p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: For “imply” questions about a distinction, ask what follows from keeping the two things apart. Here a reliable resource and cheap servicing are separate results, so having one does not guarantee the other.
p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: An option that repeats one half of a quoted distinction can be true and still miss the question. The implication lies in the gap between the two halves.

p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The writer says that the slogan “survives only in part”: “The counting-on is genuine”, but “a resource you can predict is not yet a resource you can afford”. That is partly persuaded, as B says. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s own attitude to one slogan: that tidal is the “firm” renewable, “the one you can count on”. Keep the writer’s voice apart from Toft’s and the economist’s.

steps.title: Find the verdict
steps.text: The writer’s verdict comes in the last paragraph: the slogan “survives only in part”.

steps.title: Weigh the two halves
steps.text: On one side: “The counting-on is genuine; nobody who watched the Skerrow array doubts that the current will keep its appointments.” On the other: “But a resource you can predict is not yet a resource you can afford.” The writer accepts the reliability but adds that being predictable does not yet make tidal power affordable.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B matches: dependable, but not the same as affordable. A drops “only in part”, C drops “The counting-on is genuine”, and D overlooks the writer’s own verdict.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer is partly persuaded: tidal power is dependable but not yet affordable. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer does fully accept the tide’s reliability: “The counting-on is genuine”, and nobody who watched the array doubts that the current “will keep its appointments”.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer says that the slogan “survives only in part” (step 2), so this is not full endorsement. And the text never says that tidal power has proved it can replace other sources.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer calls it a “tidy slogan” and says that it survives “only in part”, which can sound like a rejection.
distractors.why_wrong: The part that survives is exactly the dependability: “The counting-on is genuine” (step 3). The writer’s reservation is about cost, not about the tide’s reliability.

distractors.why_tempting: The middle paragraphs report Toft’s and the economist’s views side by side, which can make the writer seem neutral.
distractors.why_wrong: The last paragraph is the writer’s own verdict: the slogan “survives only in part”, and a predictable resource “is not yet a resource you can afford” (steps 2–3). A writer who gives a verdict has taken a position.

p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: For attitude questions, find where the writer judges in their own voice – often the last paragraph – and check both halves of a mixed verdict. Here the writer grants the reliability but not the affordability.
p5-elf-b6-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Do not read a mixed verdict as total agreement or total rejection. “Survives only in part” is the sign of a split verdict.

p5-elf-b6-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Roth found that in its first two seasons the lift “earned its keep less as transport than as spectacle”; on Saturday afternoons, crowds “came chiefly to be lifted”. C says the same. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Suggest” asks what the text points to about the lift in its first two seasons. Look for what the text says the lift was mainly good for in that period.

steps.title: Find the key sentence
steps.text: Reading the shop’s day-books, Roth found that “For its first two seasons the lift earned its keep less as transport than as spectacle.” To earn its keep is to be worth what it costs, and a spectacle is something people come to look at.

steps.title: Check the evidence
steps.text: The shop charged nothing to ride the lift and advertised it “rather like a fairground attraction”. On Saturday afternoons the upper-floor counters took more than the ground floor, “when crowds came chiefly to be lifted”. Roth’s closing verdict is limited to “a season or two”: in that time, “the machine sold not the floors above it but the ride itself.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C matches: the lift’s value lay more in the ride than in transport. A gives the trade press’s assumption, which Roth’s findings go against; B makes a short-lived effect permanent; and D brings in rivals that the text never mentions.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: In its first two seasons the lift mattered as a spectacle more than as transport. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: Speed is the obvious purpose of a lift, and the trade press assumed exactly that: “four floors climbed without the stairs”.
distractors.why_wrong: That was the trade press’s assumption. The day-books that Roth read told “a stranger story”: in those seasons the lift earned its keep “less as transport than as spectacle” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: For a while, the upper-floor counters really did take more than the ground floor on Saturday afternoons.
distractors.why_wrong: The text reports them taking more only on Saturday afternoons, and only for a season or two (steps 2–3). “The novelty, she notes, wore off within a few years”, and the lift then settled into a dull, useful role. Nothing suggests that the upper floors kept taking more, and the text never calls them the most profitable part of the building.

distractors.why_tempting: In a story about a successful new attraction, copying by competitors sounds like a natural next step.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions rival drapers. Roth is even “wary of drawing a rule from a single shop”.

p5-elf-b6-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “suggest” questions, find the sentence where the text sums up its finding – here “less as transport than as spectacle” – and choose the option that keeps the same contrast.
p5-elf-b6-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Do not pick the obvious purpose of a thing when the text is about a surprise. The trade press assumed speed; Roth argues that for a season or two the lift sold “the ride itself”.

p5-elf-b6-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The forecasts were good, but “The losses barely moved”: most growers already knew a frost was coming, and acting on a warning cost money and sleep. Faber suspects that what they lacked was a cheap and easy way to act. B covers all of this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the main point the text makes about the frost-warning service, so the answer must cover the whole short text, not one detail.

steps.title: Follow the set-up
steps.text: The text starts with an assumption: “better forecasts would mean fewer ruined crops”. Then: “The forecasts proved good. The losses barely moved.”

steps.title: Find the reason
steps.text: Faber found that “most orchardists already knew a hard night was on its way” and that the text message “rarely changed what they did next”. Orchardists are fruit growers. Lighting smudge pots or running wind machines, which protect the trees, “cost money and cost sleep”, and “on a borderline forecast many growers simply gambled that the frost would pass them by”. A borderline forecast is one that could go either way.

steps.title: Find Faber’s conclusion
steps.text: Faber is careful not to generalise from one valley, but suspects that the growers “were seldom short of warning, only of a cheap and easy way to act on it”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B has all three parts: good forecasts, little effect on the losses, and the real difficulty of acting on a warning. A reverses the result, C contradicts “The forecasts proved good”, and D invents a distrust of text messages.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The warnings were good but changed little; the hard part, as Faber suspects, was acting on them. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: This is the plain assumption that the text starts from: “better forecasts would mean fewer ruined crops”.
distractors.why_wrong: The text reports a different result: “The losses barely moved” (step 2). Good forecasts did not sharply cut the losses.

distractors.why_tempting: When a warning service fails, inaccurate forecasts are the usual suspect.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says “The forecasts proved good” (step 2). The trouble was not accuracy: most growers already knew a hard night was coming, and the warning rarely changed what they did (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The text mentions both the texted warnings and the radio, so a contrast between them can seem to be the point.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that the growers mistrusted text messages. The radio appears only as one of the ways that most growers already knew a frost was coming. What the text points to instead is the cost of acting: it “cost money and cost sleep” (step 3).

p5-elf-b6-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: For main-point questions about a short text, follow its shape: an expectation, a surprising result and an explanation. The right option gives the result that overturned the expectation and the explanation for it, not just the result.
p5-elf-b6-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: An option can name a familiar reason for failure, such as bad forecasts or distrust, that the text never gives. Check the reason against the text’s own explanation.

p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text sets the usual story – the neat proportion simply won – against the record: a one-vote win, a slow first year, and then a large buyer’s cabinet order that spread the size. C sums this up. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text, so the right answer must cover the main line of the argument, not one fact.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: The first paragraph gives “the usual story”: the committee simply “recognised the better geometry”. The second and third give Talvenny’s record: a vote won “by a single voice”, fewer than thirty firms after a year, and then the Wenmarch order and its cabinets. The fourth sets Ferrowby against Talvenny, and the fifth gives the writer’s verdict.

steps.title: Find the verdict
steps.text: The last paragraph says: “being the better shape did not, by itself, make it the common one.” The proportion “had to wait for a filing cabinet”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C keeps the verdict: elegance alone did not do it; a large buyer did. A gives the usual story, which the record “cuts against”, B is a detail from the first paragraph, and D builds on a detail from the second.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The folding size became the standard through a buyer’s order more than through its elegance. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: A sounds like the opening of the text, which describes the neat proportion winning.
distractors.why_wrong: That is “the usual story”, and the record goes against it. A win “by a single voice” (step 2) shows that the result was far from certain. The writer concludes that being the better shape did not by itself make it the common one (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: B is true: the first paragraph explains that each size is the one above it cut in two.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the fact the story starts from, not what the text is about. B says nothing about how the size became the standard, which is the subject of the rest of the text (steps 2–3).

distractors.why_tempting: D uses real details: the squarer sheet wasted less off the mills’ rolls, and it “had the printers behind it”.
distractors.why_wrong: These are details of the vote in the second paragraph, and D adds a reason for the printers’ choice that the text never gives. The text is mainly about how the folding size spread after it won, and D leaves that out (steps 2–3).

p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “mainly about” questions, look for the writer’s verdict, often in the last paragraph, and choose the option that states it. An option that only repeats a true detail from one paragraph is too narrow.
p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Watch out for the story a text sets up and then questions. “The usual story” in the first paragraph is what the record goes against, not the main point.

p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: Talvenny’s reading of the minutes shows that two proportions reached the last round, that the squarer one had the printers behind it and would have cost the trade less, and that “The folding sheet won the final round by a single voice”. B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks how the committee settled on the folding proportion. Look in the second paragraph, where Talvenny reports what the committee’s minutes show. Minutes are the written record of a meeting.

steps.title: Find the vote
steps.text: “Two proportions reached the last round of voting: the folding one everyone now uses, and a squarer sheet that wasted less off the standing rolls the mills already cut and would have cost the trade less to take up.”

steps.title: Find the result
steps.text: “The squarer sheet had the printers behind it. The folding sheet won the final round by a single voice”. A single voice means a single vote.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B matches: one vote, over a sheet that the printers backed and that would have cost less. A makes the win comfortable, C reverses the result, and D hands the decision to the mills.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The folding proportion won the final round by one vote. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The folding sheet did win, and the text says that the committee knew the geometry was real.
distractors.why_wrong: The committee “did not walk in agreed”, and the folding sheet won “by a single voice” (step 3). That is the opposite of a comfortable agreement from the first round.

distractors.why_tempting: The squarer sheet had real advantages, so it can seem likely that it won at first.
distractors.why_wrong: The squarer sheet lost the final round (step 3), and the text reports no earlier win for it. It also says nothing about the mills refusing to cut any shape.

distractors.why_tempting: The mills are mentioned in the description of the squarer sheet, so they seem to play a part in the decision.
distractors.why_wrong: The committee did choose: it voted, and the folding sheet won the final round (step 3). The text never says that the decision was left to the mills.

p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: For “What does the text say” questions, find the sentences that answer the question and check every detail of the option against them – here the margin of the vote, who backed the other sheet and what it would have cost.
p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Do not let the result hide the margin. The folding sheet did win, but “by a single voice”, so an option that calls the win comfortable is wrong.

p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: A year after the rule, fewer than thirty firms had taken up the standard. After the 1913 order, “Within four years the count of firms on the standard had passed six hundred.” D gives both figures. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks how take-up changed after the 1913 order. Take-up means how many firms began to use the standard, so compare the numbers before and after the order in the third paragraph.

steps.title: Before the order
steps.text: Talvenny’s count: “a year after the rule, fewer than thirty had taken it up, most of them the stationers who had sat on the committee.”

steps.title: After the order
steps.text: Then “What changed things was not the geometry, which had not moved, but a customer.” After the Wenmarch order, “Within four years the count of firms on the standard had passed six hundred.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D gives the jump from fewer than thirty to more than six hundred. A describes the slow first year, before the order; B brings in a government that the text never mentions; and C turns a count into every firm in the trade.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Take-up climbed sharply, from fewer than thirty firms to more than six hundred. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: A repeats real details: the slow first year and the committee’s own stationers.
distractors.why_wrong: Those details describe the year after the rule, before the order (step 2). After the order the count passed six hundred within four years (step 3), so take-up did not continue at the earlier pace.

distractors.why_tempting: A rule that suddenly spreads can sound like the work of a government order.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions the government. It says that what changed things was “not the geometry, which had not moved, but a customer” – the Wenmarch Assurance Office (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The direction is right, and the text says that the folding size was “suddenly the one everybody kept”.
distractors.why_wrong: The text’s hard figure is a count: the number of firms “had passed six hundred” (step 3). The phrase “the one everybody kept” is a loose way of saying that the folding size had become the usual one; it does not say that every paper-using firm in the whole trade had gone over entirely. C also has take-up rising steadily, while the text says that the proportion was “suddenly” the common one.

p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a question asks how something changed, find the figures before and after and choose the option that keeps both. Here the text gives fewer than thirty firms a year after the rule and, after the order, more than six hundred “within four years”.
p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: A true detail from the wrong time can trap you. The slow first year in A happened before the order, not after it.

p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: The office bought so many cabinets that the cabinet makers “began offering only the one size”, and a firm that bought those cabinets found that the folding sheet fitted the drawer. So the size spread through the cabinets. That is A. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Suggest” means that you must link facts the text gives. The text says what the cabinet makers did, but it does not say in so many words that this is what spread the size. The question asks how the size reached ordinary firms, beyond the Assurance Office itself, so follow the chain of events.

steps.title: Find the chain
steps.text: “The office bought paper and cabinets in such quantity that the cabinet makers, rather than tool up twice, began offering only the one size; and a firm that bought those cabinets found the folding sheet was the sheet that fitted the drawer.”

steps.title: Draw the inference
steps.text: To tool up is to set up the machines and tools for making something. The makers did not want to do that for two sizes, so they offered only the folding size. A firm that bought those cabinets got drawers that fitted the folding sheet, so buying a cabinet in effect chose the paper.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A gives this chain. B is the office’s own decision, not how the size reached other firms; C credits persuasion about geometry, which the text rules out; and D turns the makers’ choice into a physical impossibility.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The cabinets carried the size to other firms. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: B is true: the office did order its entire correspondence to be kept on the folding size.
distractors.why_wrong: That is how the office itself adopted the size. The question asks what spread it to ordinary firms after that, and the text’s answer is the cabinets (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The folding proportion has a famous geometric advantage, so persuasion sounds like a natural way for it to spread.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that the office publicised anything. It says that what changed things was “not the geometry, which had not moved, but a customer”.

distractors.why_tempting: D keeps the cabinets, which are the right idea, and makes the link sound even stronger.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says only that the makers “began offering only the one size” and that the folding sheet “was the sheet that fitted the drawer” (step 2). It never says that the cabinets could hold no other sheet, or that firms had no other option at all.

p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: For “suggest” questions about how something spread, follow the chain of cause and effect step by step. Here a large order led the makers to offer one size, and the cabinets then carried that size to other firms.
p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Do not stop at the first true sentence. B is true, but it explains how the office itself adopted the size, not how the size spread beyond it.

p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The writer’s verdict is that the record “cuts against both the tidy story and Ferrowby's version of it”: “being the better shape did not, by itself, make it the common one”. The geometry played its part but was not enough without a large buyer. That is B. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s attitude to Ferrowby’s claim. Keep three voices apart: Ferrowby, the historian Talvenny, and the writer, who gives a verdict in the last paragraph.

steps.title: Find Ferrowby’s claim
steps.text: Ferrowby says: “The maths was always going to win”, and “A proportion that good does not need a lucky customer”.

steps.title: Find Talvenny’s answer
steps.text: Talvenny agrees that the geometry was necessary but says that, on the evidence of the minutes and the returns, it was not sufficient: “Something had to make the size worth changing to, and in this case it was a drawer, not a diagram.” Necessary means it had to be there; sufficient means it was enough on its own.

steps.title: Find the writer’s verdict
steps.text: The writer concludes that the record “cuts against both the tidy story and Ferrowby's version of it”. What it shows, the writer says, is that “being the better shape did not, by itself, make it the common one.” The writer has already called Talvenny “more careful”, and this verdict follows Talvenny’s reading: the geometry was needed, but it was not enough without a large buyer.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B matches the writer’s verdict, which follows Talvenny: the geometry was needed, but not enough without a large buyer. A and C put the writer on Ferrowby’s side, and D calls the folding sheet a poor choice, which the writer rejects.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer is unconvinced by Ferrowby on the decisive point. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: A sounds as careful as B, and the writer does call the folding sheet convenient.
distractors.why_wrong: A treats the cabinet order as a mere push towards an outcome that was coming anyway, which is Ferrowby’s view. The writer says the opposite: the proportion “had to wait for a filing cabinet”, and being the better shape did not by itself make it the common one (step 4).

distractors.why_tempting: C repeats Ferrowby’s words almost exactly, and Ferrowby’s is the most confident voice in the text.
distractors.why_wrong: Those are Ferrowby’s words (step 2), not the writer’s. The writer says that the record “cuts against” Ferrowby’s version (step 4).

distractors.why_tempting: The writer does disagree with Ferrowby, so a strongly negative option can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer’s disagreement is with Ferrowby’s story, not with the sheet: “It does not show that the folding proportion was a bad choice; the sheet is convenient”. And the offices that took it up “had no reason to regret it”.

p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: For attitude questions, separate the voices first: the people quoted and the writer. Then find the writer’s verdict – here in the last paragraph – and check which side of the quoted claim it takes, and how strongly.
p5-elf-b7-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Two options can sound equally careful. A and B are both measured in tone, but A agrees with Ferrowby and B does not, so check the direction, not just the tone.

p5-elf-b7-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Bruck notes that “The scissors … force a grip that cannot be reversed; the opener and the ladle only invite one.” Left-handers managed the opener and the ladle by turning the object rather than the hand. C says this. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what difference the text draws between the scissors and the other two tools, the can opener and the ladle. The answer must be stated in the text.

steps.title: Find the results
steps.text: Left-handers “fumbled the scissors badly”, but “managed the opener and the ladle almost as smoothly as anyone once they were allowed to turn the object rather than the hand”.

steps.title: Find the distinction
steps.text: Bruck names the difference: “The scissors, she notes, force a grip that cannot be reversed; the opener and the ladle only invite one.” To invite a grip is to suggest it without forcing it, so a left-hander can work round it. With the scissors, “the upper blade hides the cut line from the left hand”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C states exactly this. A reverses which tools were hard, B says that all three were equally hard, and D puts the difference in the wrong place: the opener and the ladle also invite one way of holding them, but a left-hander can get round it by turning the object.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The scissors lock the hand into one grip; the other tools can be managed by turning the object. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The text says that some tools were hard for left-handers, and A gives a reason that sounds physical and plausible.
distractors.why_wrong: A reverses the result. The left-handers “fumbled the scissors badly” but managed the opener and the ladle “almost as smoothly as anyone” once they were allowed to turn the object (step 2). The text never mentions steadier force or a weaker hand.

distractors.why_tempting: Turning the object really did help, and B mentions it.
distractors.why_wrong: B erases the difference that the text draws. Turning the object helped with the opener and the ladle, but the scissors force a grip that “cannot be reversed” (step 3), and the left-handers fumbled them badly.

distractors.why_tempting: The scissors were the hardest tool, so it is tempting to call them the only truly right-handed one.
distractors.why_wrong: The text treats all three as right-handed tools: it opens with “The trouble with right-handed tools” and then tests openers, ladles and scissors. The word “genuinely” belongs to the tools that “lock the hand into a single approach”, and in the test that is the scissors, whose grip “cannot be reversed” (step 3). So the distinction is between a forced grip and an invited one, not between right-handed tools and other tools.

p5-elf-b7-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a question asks for a distinction, look for a sentence that sets two things against each other – here a semicolon between “force a grip that cannot be reversed” and “only invite one”. The right option keeps both sides.
p5-elf-b7-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: An option can single out the right tool and still give the wrong reason. D picks out the scissors but explains the difference in a way the text does not.

p5-elf-b7-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Iled reasons that tall grass “hides an approaching fox or hawk from the birds”, so flocking birds that will not feed where they cannot watch go elsewhere. B gives this reason. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks why, in Iled’s view, tall grass reduced the birds that most threaten aircraft. Look for the reason the text gives, not one you might guess.

steps.title: Find the result
steps.text: Bird counts on the long-grass belts “fell by roughly half”, and the flocking species “that rise in numbers into an aircraft's path” fell furthest. A sward is an area of grass, and rank grass grows thick and untidy.

steps.title: Find Iled’s reason
steps.text: “Tall grass, Iled reasons, hides an approaching fox or hawk from the birds, not the birds from anyone, so open-country flockers that will not feed where they cannot watch simply go elsewhere.” The grass blocks the birds’ view of danger, so the flocking birds that need to watch go elsewhere.

steps.title: See the turn
steps.text: Most airfields cut their grass short so that birds have “nowhere to hide”. Iled’s reasoning turns this round: what matters is not where the birds can hide but what they cannot see.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B restates Iled’s reason. A gives a food reason that the text never mentions, C invents a physical barrier, and D says that every species left, although a few solitary species were unmoved.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: In Iled’s view, the flocking birds left because the tall grass stopped them watching for predators. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: Birds come to fields to feed, so less food sounds like a natural reason for them to leave.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions insects or seeds as food. Iled’s reason is about watching for danger: these birds “will not feed where they cannot watch” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The text does mention birds rising “into an aircraft's path”, and tall, thick grass can sound like an obstacle.
distractors.why_wrong: Iled’s reason is not that the grass held the birds down. The birds “simply go elsewhere”, because they cannot watch for a fox or a hawk (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Bird counts fell a lot, so it is easy to think that all the birds left.
distractors.why_wrong: Counts fell “by roughly half”, not to nothing (step 2), and Iled notes that “a few solitary species were unmoved”. So not every species was driven away.

p5-elf-b7-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “why” questions, find the reason the text itself gives – signal words such as “reasons” and “so” help – and match the option to that reason, not to one you would expect.
p5-elf-b7-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: A food explanation sounds sensible, which is what makes A tempting. The question asks for Iled’s reason, and the text gives a different one.

p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The frame “not warmth but a faint ___” needs a feeling set against warmth, an uneasy one, and later the respondents speak of guilt and hesitation. “Apprehension”, a feeling of worry about what may happen, fits. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “the commonest reply was not warmth but a faint ___”. People were asked how an unplanned telephone call now made them feel, so the gap needs a feeling.

steps.title: Use the contrast
steps.text: “Not warmth but” sets the feeling against warmth, and the context shows which way it goes: ringing unannounced is “the very sort of intrusion”, and later the respondents speak of “guilt” and “hesitation”. Apprehension is worry or fear that something unpleasant may happen, and “a faint apprehension” is a mild form of that unease.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: All four options end in -sion, so the ending gives nothing away. “Comprehension” means understanding, “suspension” means a pause, or hanging something from above, and “dimension” means a measurement or an aspect. None of them is a feeling about a phone call.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Not warmth but a faint apprehension” is the only natural reading. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: “Comprehension” looks and sounds very like “apprehension”.
distractors.why_wrong: Comprehension means understanding. People were asked how a call made them feel, and understanding is not a feeling that can stand against warmth (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Calls that are put off leave things hanging, and “suspension” can suggest that kind of waiting.
distractors.why_wrong: Suspension means a pause, or hanging something from above; it is not a feeling. “A faint suspension” does not describe how a call makes someone feel (step 1).

distractors.why_tempting: “Dimension” can mean an aspect of something, so it can sound like a fitting abstract word.
distractors.why_wrong: A dimension is a measurement or an aspect, not a feeling. The frame sets the reply against warmth, so it needs a feeling (step 1).

p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a gap follows “not … but”, the missing word is set against the word before “but” – here “warmth”. Decide what kind of word it must be (a feeling) and which side it falls on (unpleasant), then choose.
p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Look-alike words are the trap here: apprehension, comprehension, suspension and dimension share their ending. Decide on the meaning first, then find the word that carries it.

p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The words after the dash, “the very sort of intrusion”, explain the gap: an unannounced call takes up someone’s time without asking. An unwelcome demand on someone is an imposition, so “a small imposition on their time” fits. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “had come to seem a small ___ on their time — the very sort of intrusion that a written message would have spared them”.

steps.title: Use the restatement
steps.text: After the dash, “the very sort of intrusion” restates the gap: an unannounced call is an intrusion. An imposition is an unfair or unwelcome demand on someone, and English speaks of an imposition on someone’s time. So “a small imposition on their time” fits.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: “Instruction” is an order or a piece of teaching, “injunction” is a formal order, often from a court, and “inspection” is a careful check. None of them means an intrusion on someone’s time.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “A small imposition on their time” is the only natural reading. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: “Instruction” is a familiar word with the same -ion ending as the others.
distractors.why_wrong: An instruction is an order or a piece of teaching. A friend’s call is not an order, and the frame needs a word for an intrusion (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Injunction” is a formal word that sounds like a strong demand.
distractors.why_wrong: An injunction is a formal order, usually from a court. A friend’s call is not a legal order, and the word does not mean an intrusion (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Being checked on can feel intrusive, and an inspection is a kind of check.
distractors.why_wrong: An inspection is a careful examination. A call does not examine someone’s time; it takes up that time uninvited, which is what an imposition does (step 2).

p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: When a dash follows the gap, read what comes after it: it often restates or explains the missing word. Here “the very sort of intrusion” tells you that the gap means an unwelcome demand.
p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: All four nouns are formal words ending in -ion, so the ending does not help. Test each one in the whole phrase “a small ___ on their time”.

p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The gapped sentence grants an obvious point – some of this is plain convenience – before “But” turns to the deeper mood. A connective that grants a point in this way is “Admittedly”. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens the sentence “___, some of this is plain convenience.” Two sentences later comes “But the mood his respondents describe is far from ___.”

steps.title: Find the relationship
steps.text: The gapped sentence grants a simple explanation for the drift away from calls: messages are convenient. Then “But” brings in what really troubles the respondents: guilt and hesitation. A sentence that grants a point before a “But” is a concession, and “Admittedly” marks a concession.

steps.title: Check the other connectives
steps.text: “Consequently” means as a result, “Meanwhile” means at the same time, and “Conversely” introduces the opposite. Convenience is offered as part of the explanation for the drift, not as its result; nothing else happens at the same time; and the sentence does not state an opposite.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Admittedly, some of this is plain convenience” sets up the “But” that follows. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence before reports a change, so a word for a result can seem to follow.
distractors.why_wrong: “Consequently” would make convenience a result of the roughly halved share. In fact convenience is offered as part of the explanation for the drift, granted before the “But” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Meanwhile” is a common linking word at the start of a paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: “Meanwhile” brings in something happening at the same time, or another side of the situation; it does not grant a point. This sentence grants one, which the “But” sentence then moves past (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph contrasts messages with calls, so a word for the opposite can seem right.
distractors.why_wrong: “Conversely” introduces the opposite of what came before. Convenience is not the opposite of the drift away from calls; it is one reason for it, granted before the turn (step 2).

p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a gapped sentence is soon followed by “But”, test a concession word such as “Admittedly”: the sentence grants a point, and the “But” moves past it.
p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Connectives all look alike as sentence openers. Work out how the sentence relates to its neighbours – result, time, opposite or concession – before you choose.

p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: “Far from ___” means not at all, and “instead” shows that the real mood is guilt and hesitation. So the gap needs the happy opposite: “far from jubilant”. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “But the mood his respondents describe is far from ___.” The next sentence begins: “They speak instead of guilt, of hesitation, of calls quietly put off for weeks”.

steps.title: Work out the direction
steps.text: “Far from” means not at all, and “instead” tells you that the gap names the opposite of guilt and hesitation. Jubilant means very happy, as when celebrating, so “far from jubilant” means not at all happy – a mood of guilt and hesitation.

steps.title: Check the other adjectives
steps.text: “Hesitant” and “reluctant” describe the mood that the respondents actually report, so “far from hesitant” or “far from reluctant” would say the opposite of the next sentence. “Resonant” means deep and echoing, or rich in meaning, which is not the opposite of guilt.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Far from jubilant” – not happy at all – leads into the guilt and hesitation that follow. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: “Resonant” can describe something that stirs feeling, and the respondents do describe feelings about calls: guilt and hesitation.
distractors.why_wrong: Resonant means deep and echoing, or rich in meaning. It is not the opposite of guilt and hesitation, which is what “far from” and “instead” call for (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Hesitant” echoes “hesitation” in the very next sentence, so it seems to match.
distractors.why_wrong: “Hesitant” echoes “hesitation”, and that is the trap: “far from hesitant” would mean bold and sure, but the next sentence says that the respondents speak of hesitation (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The respondents put calls off for weeks, which does sound reluctant.
distractors.why_wrong: Putting calls off does sound reluctant, and that is exactly why C is wrong: “far from reluctant” would mean eager, which clashes with calls put off for weeks (steps 1 and 3).

p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: In a “far from ___” frame, the gap names the opposite of what is really true. Read the sentence after it – here “They speak instead of guilt, of hesitation” – and choose the word for the opposite mood.
p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: A word that echoes the text can be a trap. “Hesitant” matches “hesitation”, but after “far from” it means the reverse.

p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: An assumption that falls out of use is said to lapse, and “quietly” fits a change that came without fuss. So “has, Vinderhed suggests, quietly lapsed” is the natural reading. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “The old assumption that a voice was the warmest way to reach another person has, Vinderhed suggests, quietly ___.” The subject is an assumption, and “quietly” says that the change happened without fuss.

steps.title: Find the verb
steps.text: To lapse is to come to an end gradually or fall out of use, as a habit, a custom or a membership can. The text describes such a drift: across a decade the share of adults who said they would rather be telephoned “has roughly halved”. So “quietly lapsed” fits both the subject and a change that came without fuss.

steps.title: Check the look-alikes
steps.text: All four options end in -lapsed. To collapse is to fail suddenly and completely, which suits a drift across a decade less well than lapse does. Elapse is used for periods of time passing, not for beliefs. To relapse is to fall back into an illness or a bad habit after getting better.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Has, Vinderhed suggests, quietly lapsed” fits the change the text describes. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: “Collapsed” is a strong word for an idea that no longer holds, and it shares most of its letters with the key.
distractors.why_wrong: To collapse is to fail suddenly and completely. The text describes a drift instead: across a decade the share who would rather be telephoned “has roughly halved” (step 2). An assumption that fades out of use like this is better said to have lapsed.

distractors.why_tempting: “Elapsed” suggests time passing, and the text describes a change over a decade.
distractors.why_wrong: Elapse is used for periods of time, not for beliefs: time elapses, but an assumption does not. The subject of the gap is “The old assumption” (step 1).

distractors.why_tempting: “Relapsed” suggests going backwards, which can sound like a change for the worse.
distractors.why_wrong: To relapse is to fall back into an illness or a bad habit after improving. An assumption that is fading away is not falling back into an earlier state (step 3).

p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: When the options look alike, use the other words in the frame and the text around it. Here the subject (“The old assumption”) and the drift across a decade point to a verb for falling out of use.
p5-elf-b8-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Look-alike verbs differ in meaning: collapsed, lapsed, elapsed and relapsed share most of their letters. Check each one against the subject and against the change the text describes.

p5-elf-b8-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text says that Sunde “wanted the guest's credential to expire”: the lock could be told to forget a card’s code the moment the guest checked out. B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for Sunde’s main aim, as the text states it. Look for the sentence that names the aim, and keep it apart from what came later.

steps.title: Find the aim
steps.text: “His aim was narrower than that. He wanted the guest's credential to expire”. A credential is something that proves you may enter – here the card – and to expire is to stop being valid.

steps.title: See how it worked
steps.text: The card carried “a code the lock could be told to forget the instant the guest checked out, so that the next arrival's card opened a door the previous card no longer would.” This answers the brass key’s flaw: a guest who copied a key, or did not hand it back, “could let himself in again months later”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B states the aim. A describes the swipe, which came “afterward, and largely by accident”; C makes cost-cutting the aim, which the text never says; and D brings in a record of entries that the text never mentions.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Sunde wanted each card to stop working once the guest left. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The smooth swipe is what most people now think of as the point of a keycard.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says that Sunde “did not set out to save anyone a walk to the front desk”, and that “The smooth swipe and the tidy wallet came afterward, and largely by accident.” Convenience was a side effect, not the aim.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does say that re-cutting every lock was “ruinously expensive”, so saving money can seem to be the point.
distractors.why_wrong: The cost of re-cutting locks is part of the brass key’s problem, but the text never says that Sunde aimed to cut costs, and it never calls the cards cheap. It names the aim directly: the credential should expire (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Modern keycard systems can record entries, so D sounds like something a keycard lock might be for.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions any record of which rooms a guest entered. The aim it gives is that each card should stop working at checkout (step 3).

p5-elf-b8-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a question asks for someone’s aim, look for the words that announce it – here “His aim was narrower than that.” – and read the next sentence, which names it: “He wanted the guest's credential to expire”. Keep the aim apart from effects that came later.
p5-elf-b8-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: A later benefit is not the same as the original aim. The text says that the swipe and the tidy wallet came “afterward, and largely by accident”.

p5-elf-b8-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text says that what “actually grinds a marking away is the grit and road salt that passing traffic drags across it and, on northern roads, the steel edge of the snowplough”. Tyres hardly touch the line, and the same paint can last for years on a quiet lane. A says this. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what mainly decides how long a road marking stays serviceable – that is, still good enough to use. Look for the cause the text itself names.

steps.title: Set aside the usual guess
steps.text: The text first rules out the cause most people picture: “A tyre almost never passes directly over the painted line; cars straddle it, one wheel to each side.” To straddle something is to have one part on each side of it.

steps.title: Find the real cause
steps.text: “What actually grinds a marking away is the grit and road salt that passing traffic drags across it and, on northern roads, the steel edge of the snowplough.”

steps.title: Check the comparison
steps.text: That explains why the same paint lasts so differently. On a quiet country lane, “spared both heavy traffic and the plough”, a line may still be serviceable “well into the next” decade, while on a motorway it is repainted three or four times a year. So age is not what decides.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A names the grit, the salt and the plough. B gives the tyres that the text rules out, C brings in sun and rain, which the text never mentions, and D blames the paint, although the text says that “the same paint” behaves differently from place to place.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Wear from grit and salt and, on northern roads, the plough decides how long a marking lasts. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: Tyres grinding the paint down is the picture most people have.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says that a tyre “almost never passes directly over the painted line” (step 2). The grinding comes from grit and salt and, on northern roads, the plough (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Sun and rain wear down most things left outdoors, so weathering sounds like an obvious cause.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions sunlight or rain. The causes it names are grit and salt and, on northern roads, the plough (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Cheaper materials often wear out sooner, so the grade of paint sounds like a sensible explanation.
distractors.why_wrong: The text speaks of “the same paint” behaving differently from place to place, and it never mentions grades of paint or saving money (step 4).

p5-elf-b8-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a text sets aside a common belief with words such as “though” or “actually”, the answer usually lies in what follows. Here “What actually grinds a marking away” introduces the real cause.
p5-elf-b8-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Do not choose the cause you would have guessed. The text corrects the usual guess about tyres.

p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text reports a nine-year study that put the usual case for beavers – storage volume – to the test. In ordinary storms the ponds did lower the peaks, but in the largest storms what mattered was where the dams were, while their volume predicted almost nothing. C covers both halves. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text. The right answer must cover the main line of the argument, not one scene or one result.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: The first paragraph sets out the usual case: dams store water, and storage is “the figure quoted at consultations”. It ends: “What it assumes is that a flood peak is made of volume. It is made of timing.” The second paragraph shows the ponds lowering the peaks of ordinary storms. The third shows that in the largest storms the drop in peak height “bore almost no relation to how much water the dams upstream could hold”. The fourth sets Traer against Sorrel, and the fifth gives the writer’s verdict.

steps.title: Find the verdict
steps.text: The writer concludes that volume, “when the water is high … predicts very little”, while “How the dams are spread across a catchment's tributaries is awkward to measure and predicts a good deal.” A catchment is the land that drains into one river, and its tributaries are the streams that feed it.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C keeps both halves: the ponds help in ordinary storms, and in the rarest storms the spread of the dams counts, not their volume. A criticises the volunteers’ measuring, which the text never does; B brings in the value of wetlands, which the text never discusses; and D turns a result from two of fourteen storms into a general rule.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about what beaver dams do to floods: they help in ordinary storms, and in the largest ones their spread matters more than their volume. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The first paragraph mentions volunteers adding up storage “in hectare-metres” with tape measures, and the text is critical of the storage figure.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that the volunteers measure badly. Its complaint is about the figure itself: volume is “easy to measure”, but when the water is high it predicts very little (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Wetland value is a common argument for bringing beavers back, so it sounds like it could be the deeper point.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never discusses wetlands or their value. It stays with floods: peaks, timing, volume and where the dams sit (steps 2 and 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The text does report that in two of the fourteen largest storms the gauge read “a little higher” than before the beavers.
distractors.why_wrong: Two storms out of fourteen, and only “a little higher”, is a side result, not a general rule and not the main point. The text also covers the ordinary storms, in which the ponds helped (step 2).

p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “mainly about” questions on a long text, look for the sentence where the writer sums up – here in the last paragraph – and check that the option covers both the part that confirms the usual view and the part that unsettles it.
p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Watch out for an option that turns a small result into a rule. Two storms out of fourteen, with a peak only “a little higher”, cannot carry the whole text.

p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The second paragraph says that in the ordinary winter storms the peak at the gauge “was lower than before the beavers, and it arrived later”, and that “That held in all eleven sub-catchments”. A says this. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the text says about the ordinary winter storms – “the ones that come six or seven times a winter”. They are described in the second paragraph; the rare storms come later.

steps.title: Find the result
steps.text: “the peak that reached the gauge at Millstake was lower than before the beavers, and it arrived later. That held in all eleven sub-catchments, the steep peaty ones and the gentle grazed ones alike.” A sub-catchment is a smaller area that drains into one stream, and a gauge measures how high the river runs.

steps.title: Keep the two kinds of storm apart
steps.text: The text’s other main result – that the drop in peak height “bore almost no relation to how much water the dams upstream could hold” – belongs to the fourteen largest events, not to the ordinary storms. In the ordinary storms “the ponds do the obvious work”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A keeps both points: lower and later, in all eleven. B contradicts “all eleven”, C belongs to the largest storms, and D describes a kind of pond management that the text never mentions.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: In ordinary storms the peak was lower and later in every sub-catchment. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: B sounds careful, and careful options are often right.
distractors.why_wrong: Here the text is not cautious: the result “held in all eleven sub-catchments, the steep peaty ones and the gentle grazed ones alike” (step 2). B’s exception for the steep peaty ones contradicts that.

distractors.why_tempting: C repeats a real finding, but about other storms: across the fourteen largest events, the drop in peak height “bore almost no relation” to the volume the dams could hold.
distractors.why_wrong: That was true of the fourteen largest events, not of the ordinary storms (step 3). The text says it was in the largest storms “that stored volume stopped predicting anything”, not in the ordinary ones.

distractors.why_tempting: Drawing ponds down before a storm sounds like a sensible way to make room for rain.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that anyone managed the ponds. Sorrel’s group let the dams build up “as the colonies saw fit”.

p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: When a text gives one result for ordinary cases and another for rare ones, check which group the question names. Here “ordinary winter storms” points to the second paragraph.
p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Do not reach for the cautious-sounding option by habit. When the text says “all eleven”, an option with an exception is wrong.

p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The text says that once the rain has run long enough for every pond in a sub-catchment to fill – about forty hours in the Ferrow – “the freeboard is gone, and the water is passed down much as it would have been before the animals came back.” D says this. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about long spells of rain. Look for the sentence about rain that goes on for a long time: it comes at the end of the third paragraph.

steps.title: Find the sentence
steps.text: “There is a ceiling on it in any case. Once the rain has run long enough for every pond in a sub-catchment to fill — about forty hours in the Ferrow — the freeboard is gone, and the water is passed down much as it would have been before the animals came back.”

steps.title: Explain the words
steps.text: A ceiling is an upper limit. Freeboard, as the note under the text explains, is the empty depth left in a pond before it spills. So once every pond in a sub-catchment is full, the ponds can hold no more, and the water flows on much as it did before the beavers came.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D restates this. A reverses the travel times, B invents dams that burst, and C has the beavers abandon their highest ponds, which the text never mentions.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: In long rain the ponds fill up, and after that the water passes through much as it did before. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does compare how long water takes to arrive from the highest and the lowest tributaries.
distractors.why_wrong: It says the opposite: water entering the highest tributary “takes the better part of a day longer to reach Millstake” than water entering the lowest. So the higher water arrives later, not sooner.

distractors.why_tempting: Dams bursting under the weight of water is a natural thing to fear in a long storm.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that the dams give way. It says that once every pond in a sub-catchment is full, “the freeboard is gone” and the water is passed down (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: It sounds like the kind of thing animals might do when the water rises.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that the beavers leave their ponds or move downstream when the rain goes on. It says only that the ponds fill until “the freeboard is gone” (step 2).

p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: For “What are we told” questions, find the sentence about the named topic – here long rain – and match the option to it. Here “There is a ceiling on it in any case” marks a limit on the result just reported, and the sentence that starts with “Once” says when that limit is reached.
p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Do not fill a gap in the text with what you would expect to happen, such as dams bursting. The text gives a quieter answer: the ponds simply fill up.

p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: Water from tributaries of unequal length takes different times to reach the gauge, so water held back by dams spread across several tributaries arrives at different times and the flows are less likely to peak together; a chain on one tributary works on “a single schedule”. B draws this link. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Suggest” means that the text does not state the answer in one sentence. Start from Sorrel’s point about the length of the tributaries and work out the one step that follows.

steps.title: Find the premise
steps.text: Sorrel points out that “water entering the highest of them takes the better part of a day longer to reach Millstake than water entering the lowest; a chain of ponds on one tributary fills, spills and empties on a single schedule.”

steps.title: Link it to the result
steps.text: The text has just reported that “Where colonies had spread across several tributaries, the peak was blunted more often than not”, while a chain holding a similar volume on a single tributary did not blunt it. To blunt a peak is to make it lower and flatter.

steps.title: Draw the inference
steps.text: Water from different tributaries takes different times to reach the gauge. So when dams are spread across several tributaries, the water they hold back reaches the gauge at different times, and the flows are less likely to peak together. A chain on one tributary “fills, spills and empties on a single schedule”. Sorrel offers this only cautiously – the text says that Sorrel “will not push the explanation far” – and the last sentence keeps a limit too: “On the Ferrow, at least”, the beavers did not so much hold a flood back “as take it apart”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B states the link. A ranks the tributaries by how much water they carry, which the text never does; C brings in a difference in volume, but the text compares a chain and spread-out dams that hold “a similar volume”; and D says that water from the higher tributaries arrives too late to count in the recorded peak, which the text never says.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Different travel times help spread-out dams keep the flood peaks apart. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: It sounds reasonable that a longer stream gathers more water, and A uses the idea of length from the question.
distractors.why_wrong: The text compares the tributaries by their length and by how long their water takes to reach Millstake, never by how much water they carry (step 2). It never says that the dams on the longest ones do most of the work.

distractors.why_tempting: Storage volume is the figure the usual argument is built on, so a difference in how much the dams hold can seem to explain the result.
