distractors.why_wrong: The text compares a single chain with spread-out dams holding “a similar volume” of pond. The volume was about the same; what differed was where the dams were (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: D starts from a true point: water entering the highest tributary takes “the better part of a day longer” to reach Millstake than water entering the lowest.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that water from the higher tributaries arrives too late to count in the peak the gauge records. It mentions the longer travel time as part of Sorrel’s cautious explanation of a result about the dams: where colonies had spread across several tributaries, the peak was blunted “more often than not” (steps 2–4). D leaves the dams out.

p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: When a question asks what the text suggests follows from a fact, take the stated fact – here unequal travel times – and join it to a result the text reports nearby – here spread-out dams blunting the peak. The right answer is the one-step link between them.
p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Do not fall back on volume. Across the fourteen largest events in the record, similar volumes of pond gave different results, and the drop in peak height tracked where the dams were rather than how much they held.

p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The writer grants that the ponds do real work in ordinary storms: the record “does not make the animals decorative”. But a flood defence is built for the rare storm, and in those storms stored volume “stopped predicting anything”. A real gain, but too narrow to replace engineered defences – that is C. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s attitude to Traer’s case. Keep the voices apart: Traer, Sorrel and the writer, whose verdict comes in the last paragraph.

steps.title: Find Traer’s case
steps.text: Traer says: “Every dam is a flood defence, and every pond is money the council does not have to spend on concrete.” In other words, beavers can take the place of engineered flood defences.

steps.title: Find what the writer grants
steps.text: “It does not make the animals decorative: in the ordinary storms the ponds do the obvious work, and the reduction is real enough for the people at the bottom of the valley to feel it in a wet January.”

steps.title: Find the writer’s limit
steps.text: But a defence at the bottom of a valley, the writer points out, “is not built for the rain that comes six times a season but for the storm that comes once in a working life”, and in those storms stored volume “stopped predicting anything”. The text also sets a ceiling: once every pond in a sub-catchment is full – “about forty hours in the Ferrow” – the water is passed down “much as it would have been before the animals came back”. The writer’s verdict is that the record “is more divided than either side's leaflet”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C matches: something real is granted, but the gain is too narrow to replace engineered defences. A gives Traer’s own view to the writer, B says that the record bears out the leaflets, and D calls the benefit too slight to matter, which the writer rejects.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer grants the beavers a real but limited benefit, not one that can stand in for engineered defences. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: A repeats Traer’s words closely, and they are the most forceful words in the text.
distractors.why_wrong: These are Traer’s words, not the writer’s (step 2). The writer’s verdict is that the record “is more divided than either side's leaflet” (step 4), which is not acceptance.

distractors.why_tempting: B sounds balanced, and the writer does take Sorrel’s caution seriously.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer does not conclude that the record bears the leaflets out. It is “more divided than either side's leaflet” (step 4), and the storage figure the leaflets rely on “predicts very little” when the water is high.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer questions the campaigners’ favourite figure, which can sound like a dismissal of the whole campaign.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer says the opposite: the record “does not make the animals decorative”, and the reduction in ordinary storms is “real enough” for people to feel (step 3).

p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For attitude questions, find the writer’s own verdict and check what it grants and what it limits. Here the writer grants a real benefit in ordinary storms but sets limits on it in the largest ones.
p5-elf-b9-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Do not give a quoted person’s view to the writer. Traer’s words are the most memorable in the text, but they are Traer’s, and the writer’s verdict is more divided.

p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: A queue has no warden, no charter and no penalty clause, yet people obey it. An unwritten rule that people follow without any law is a convention, so a queue is among “the most reliably obeyed conventions in public life”. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “A queue has no warden, no charter and no penalty clause, and yet it remains among the most reliably obeyed ___ in public life.”

steps.title: Use the clue
steps.text: “No warden, no charter and no penalty clause” means that no official keeps order in the queue, no written document sets it up and there is no formal punishment. Yet people obey it. A convention is an unwritten rule of behaviour that people follow because everyone does, so “obeyed conventions” fits.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: “Convictions” are firm personal beliefs, “concessions” are things granted or given up, as in a bargain, and “connections” are links. None of them is a shared rule that people can obey.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Among the most reliably obeyed conventions in public life” is the only natural reading. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: “Convictions” are strongly held, and the queue is reliably obeyed, so the word can sound strong enough.
distractors.why_wrong: A conviction is a firmly held belief. The sentence says what a queue itself is: one of “the most reliably obeyed ___ in public life”. A queue is not a belief at all; it is a custom that everyone present shares and follows (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: People in a queue do give way to each other, which can feel like making concessions.
distractors.why_wrong: A concession is something granted or given up, as in a bargain. The sentence needs a rule that people obey, and nobody obeys a concession (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A queue links people together in a line, so “connections” can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: Connections are links between people or things. They cannot be obeyed, and the sentence is about an unwritten rule (step 2).

p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a sentence says what something lacks – here a warden, a charter and a penalty clause – ask what kind of thing it still is. A shared rule that people obey although no law or official enforces it is a convention.
p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: All four options start with con- and end in -ions, so they look alike. Choose by meaning: only one names a shared rule of behaviour.

p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The gap must name something shared: the belief “that everybody present will keep the place they took”. Something people take for granted without proof is an assumption, so “a shared assumption” fits. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “The whole arrangement runs on little more than a shared ___ that everybody present will keep the place they took.”

steps.title: Find the noun
steps.text: The words after the gap, “that everybody present will keep the place they took”, give the content of the missing noun: something people take for granted about each other. An assumption is something you believe without proof, and a shared assumption is one that everybody makes. That also fits the first sentence: no warden, charter or penalty clause enforces the queue.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: “Resumption” means starting again, “gumption” means good sense or the courage to act, and “consumption” means using something up. None of them can be a belief about what everybody will do.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “A shared assumption that everybody present will keep the place they took” is the only natural reading. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: “Resumption” differs from “assumption” by only a few letters, so it is easy to pick by eye.
distractors.why_wrong: A resumption is the starting again of something that had stopped. It is not a belief, so it cannot be followed by “that everybody present will keep the place they took” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Gumption” is a lively word, and it can take some nerve to hold your place in a queue.
distractors.why_wrong: Gumption means good sense or the courage to act. It is a quality that people have, not a belief about what everybody will do (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The queues in the text form at bakeries and ticket halls, where people buy things, so a word about consumption can seem connected.
distractors.why_wrong: Consumption means using things up, such as food or energy. It cannot carry the meaning “that everybody present will keep the place they took” (step 2).

p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: When the gap is followed by a that-clause that gives the content of the noun – here “that everybody present will keep the place they took” – the noun must be one that can have such content, such as an assumption, a belief or a hope. Test each option with the whole clause.
p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Rhyming options – resumption, assumption, gumption, consumption – invite a choice by sound. Read the clause after the gap and choose by meaning.

p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The sentence before gives evidence: a counter approached from two sides caused far more disputes than a roped corridor. The gapped sentence draws a conclusion from it – the room itself does much of the moral work. A connective for a conclusion that follows from evidence is “Accordingly”. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens “___, the room itself does a good deal of the moral work that we prefer to credit to the people standing in it.” The sentence before reports Mautner’s finding: “a counter approached from two sides, she found, produced more open disputes in an afternoon than a roped corridor produced in a month.”

steps.title: Find the relationship
steps.text: The finding shows that the layout of a place changes how people behave. The gapped sentence states what follows from that finding: the room does a good deal of the moral work. A conclusion drawn from evidence is introduced by “Accordingly”, which means so, or as a result.

steps.title: Check the other connectives
steps.text: “Admittedly” admits a point that goes against the main argument, “Conversely” introduces the opposite, and “Nevertheless” introduces something that is true in spite of what came before. The gapped sentence does none of these: it follows from the evidence.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Accordingly, the room itself does a good deal of the moral work” draws the conclusion. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: “Admittedly” is a common way to open a sentence in an argument, and the claim about the room is surprising.
distractors.why_wrong: “Admittedly” introduces a point that goes against the main argument. Here the sentence supports it: it is the conclusion that the dispute figures point to (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence contrasts the room with the people in it, so a contrast word can seem right.
distractors.why_wrong: “Conversely” would introduce the opposite of the sentence before. The gapped sentence does not reverse the finding; it draws a conclusion from it (step 2). The contrast with the people lies inside the sentence, not between the two sentences.

distractors.why_tempting: “Nevertheless” sounds weighty and fits many sentences in an essay.
distractors.why_wrong: “Nevertheless” means in spite of what came before. Nothing in the finding stands against the claim about the room; the finding supports it (step 2).

p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: For a connective gap, compare the gapped sentence with the one before it. If the earlier sentence gives evidence and the gapped one draws a lesson from it, choose a result word such as “Accordingly”.
p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: A contrast inside the gapped sentence – the room against the people – can pull you towards a contrast connective. The connective links this sentence to the one before, so judge that link.

p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: The gap names what one might expect to keep a queue together, and the text denies it: the people are cold and impatient and hold their places because “the alternative is to be looked at”. Politeness is not what keeps them in line, so the gap is “courtesy”. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “What keeps a line intact, on her evidence, is not ___ at all.” Whatever fills it, the text says that it is not what keeps a queue together.

steps.title: Use the next sentence
steps.text: “The people in it are cold, impatient and privately sure that the counter could be staffed better; they hold their places anyway, because the alternative is to be looked at.” What keeps them in line is that otherwise they would be looked at. Courtesy means politeness and good manners. It is the obvious explanation, and the text denies it.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: “Hostility” means unfriendliness, “vanity” means too much pride in yourself, and “curiosity” means wanting to know things. Vanity and curiosity are not usual explanations for queuing, so denying them would make no point. And “not hostility at all” would clash with the text: the small sanctions it describes – a cough, a stare – are unfriendly signals, and they “are usually enough”.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Not courtesy at all”: people hold their places because the alternative is to be looked at, not out of politeness. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: “Impatient” comes in the very next sentence, so a negative word like “hostility” can seem to match the mood.
distractors.why_wrong: “Not hostility at all” would clash with the text: what keeps order is small, unfriendly sanctions – “a cough, a stare held half a second too long” – which “are usually enough” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: People do care how they look to others in a queue, which can sound like vanity.
distractors.why_wrong: Vanity is too much pride in your own looks or abilities. The text never suggests that anyone queues out of vanity, so “not vanity at all” would deny something nobody had claimed (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: People in a queue watch each other closely, which can look like curiosity.
distractors.why_wrong: Curiosity is the wish to know things. Nobody suggests that curiosity holds a queue together, so denying it would make no point (step 3). The text’s point is about why people hold their places: because the alternative is to be looked at (step 2).

p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: In a “not ___ at all” frame, the gap names an explanation that the text rejects. Find what the text offers instead – here being looked at – and choose the word it replaces.
p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: The negative mood around the gap – cold, impatient – can pull you towards a negative word. But the frame denies the gap word, so you need the pleasant explanation that the text rejects.

p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: Newcomers “read the shape of a line”, and a queue breaks down when people can no longer read it. Something that can be read is legible, so the shape “stopped being legible”. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “It is because the shape stopped being ___”, and the examples follow: a second till opened, a rope was moved, a doorway offered two ways in. Then people “no longer agreed about where the line was”.

steps.title: Find the clue
steps.text: The first paragraph says that newcomers “read the shape of a line” and that “Where that shape is ambiguous, the trouble starts”. Legible means clear enough to read. A shape that stopped being legible is one that people could no longer read – the trouble the examples describe.

steps.title: Check the look-alikes
steps.text: “Illegible” means impossible to read, so “stopped being illegible” would mean that the shape became clear – the opposite. “Eligible” means qualified to be chosen, and “negligible” means too small to matter. Neither describes a shape that people read.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “The shape stopped being legible”: people could no longer read where the line was. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: “Eligible” looks and sounds like “legible”.
distractors.why_wrong: Eligible means qualified to be chosen, as for a job or a prize. A queue’s shape is not chosen; it is read (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Illegible” is the reading word most people know, and the queue does become hard to read.
distractors.why_wrong: The queue does become hard to read, and that is exactly why B is wrong: a shape that became hard to read “stopped being legible”. “Stopped being illegible” would mean that it became readable, the opposite of the breakdown (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: “Negligible” is another look-alike, and the text calls the sanctions in a queue small.
distractors.why_wrong: Negligible means too small to matter. The sentence is about whether people can read the shape, not about its size (step 2).

p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: When a text sets up an image – here reading the shape of a line – a later gap often completes it. Look back for the image before choosing between look-alike words.
p5-elf-b9-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Watch the negative prefix together with “stopped being”. A shape that became unreadable stopped being legible, not illegible.

p5-elf-b9-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The stripes come from the roller: grass pressed away from you “reads as pale”, and grass pressed towards you “reads as dark”. From the opposite stand every band is seen from the other direction, so pale and dark swap, “though not a blade has moved.” A says this. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks why, according to the text, the same pitch is never quite the same pitch twice when you move to the opposite stand. The reason comes just before. The sentence that reports Torvund’s saying opens with “Which is why”, and that phrase points back to the reason.

steps.title: Find the mechanism
steps.text: The stripes “are laid after the blade has passed, by the heavy roller behind it: grass pressed away from you throws the light back and reads as pale, grass pressed towards you swallows it and reads as dark.”

steps.title: Apply it to the far stand
steps.text: From the opposite stand, grass that was pressed away from you is now pressed towards you, and the other way round. So “every pale band has gone dark and every dark band pale, though not a blade has moved.” The text sums up: “The pattern is not in the grass. It is in the angle you happen to be standing at.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A gives this reason: the bands come from the way the grass lies, so they read the other way round from the far side. B makes the far half always look darker, which the text never says; C brings in lighting; and D says that the rows are cut to two heights, which the first sentence denies.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The same rows read the other way round from the far side. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The roller is the real cause of the stripes, and B mentions it.
distractors.why_wrong: The roller presses the bands in different directions; it does not tip the whole pitch towards one end (step 2). And the text never says that the far half looks darker: the pattern runs in stripes, not halves, and a spectator down at pitch level “may find almost no pattern there at all”.

distractors.why_tempting: Light really does change how grass looks, and the text is about light being thrown back or swallowed.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions floodlights or the sun’s angle. The change it describes comes from where you stand, not from the lighting (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Cutting the grass to different heights sounds like a natural way to make stripes.
distractors.why_wrong: The text opens by ruling this out: “nothing is cut to two heights”. It never mentions soil either.

p5-elf-b9-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “why” questions, look for the explanation the text gives just before or after the claim – signals such as “Which is why” point to it – and choose the option that restates that cause.
p5-elf-b9-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Options that make the pattern a fixed feature of the pitch – rows cut to two heights – or that bring in something the text never says – the lighting, a far half that always looks darker – miss the text’s point: “not a blade has moved”, and what changes is “the angle you happen to be standing at”.

p5-elf-b9-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: A surface is built “to bring a falling head to rest slowly enough”, and how slowly depends on “the tallest platform standing above it”. A bed of chips must also be raked back, or it may lose depth. C covers both. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what decides whether a playground surface is safe enough. “According to the text” means that the answer is stated there.

steps.title: Set aside the usual idea
steps.text: The text opens: “A playground surface is not engineered to feel soft.” So softness underfoot is not the test.

steps.title: Find the real test
steps.text: “It is engineered to bring a falling head to rest slowly enough, and how slowly is decided by the tallest platform standing above it.” So the same bed can pass under a low toddler frame and “fail badly under a three-meter tower”.

steps.title: Add the upkeep
steps.text: The material alone does not decide: poured rubber and wood chips “can both be built to meet the same fall height”. But chips get kicked out from under the swings, and “a bed that met its rating in May may be two inches short of it by September unless somebody rakes it back”. So the bed must also be kept deep enough.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C names both conditions: how gently the surface stops a falling head, measured against the tallest equipment, and keeping it deep enough. A ranks the materials, although the text says that both can meet the same fall height; B is the idea the text opens by rejecting; and D brings in drainage, which the text never mentions.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Safety depends on stopping a fall gently enough for the height, and on keeping the bed deep enough. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: Poured rubber sounds modern and costly, and loose fills such as bark can seem like the cheap option.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says that the loose fills are “neither the cheap compromise nor the villain they are usually taken for”, and that rubber and chips “can both be built to meet the same fall height” (step 4). So the material alone does not decide.

distractors.why_tempting: A soft surface sounds like the obvious thing to want under a playground.
distractors.why_wrong: The text opens by rejecting this: “A playground surface is not engineered to feel soft” (step 2). It is judged by how slowly it brings a falling head to rest (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Wet ground can pack down hard, so drainage sounds like a sensible safety concern.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions drainage or waterlogging. The way a bed loses its rating, in the text, is that the chips are kicked away and not raked back (step 4).

p5-elf-b9-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a text opens by saying what something is not – here “not engineered to feel soft” – the next sentence usually says what it is. Base your answer on that sentence and on any condition the text adds later.
p5-elf-b9-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Do not stop at the first condition. The text adds a second one at the end: a bed of chips must be raked back, or it may end up “two inches short” of its rating.

p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text argues that the commissioning figure “says nothing about year ten”: a damper’s benefit fades as the building drifts but can be restored, while a shape’s benefit does not fade but cannot be restored once the wind around it changes. B sums this up. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text, so the answer must cover its main line, not one tower or one person’s view.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: The first paragraph opens with the Verrand’s damper and its visitors, and introduces the commissioning figure – the reduction measured when a new tower is handed over – which “describes one afternoon”. The second shows that dampers do work as promised at first. The third shows their benefit fading as buildings gain mass, and coming back when a damper is retuned. The fourth turns to towers shaped against the wind, which “do not drift” but can be harmed by a new building upwind. The fifth compares the two approaches.

steps.title: Find the verdict
steps.text: “So the damper's advantage decays and can be restored; the shape's advantage does not decay and cannot be. Neither is obviously the safer bet”. The commissioning figure “says nothing about year ten”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B matches: the two approaches differ in what happens after handover. A turns the Verrand’s damper into a failure, which the text never says; C picks a winner, although the text says that neither is obviously the safer bet; and D raises wind loads and design margins, which the text never discusses.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about how the two ways of steadying a tower fare after handover. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The text opens with the Verrand’s damper and its visitors, and later shows that dampers lose much of their benefit.
distractors.why_wrong: The fading benefit is a finding across nineteen towers in Brayle. For the Verrand the text gives only the commissioning figure and no later measurement, and it describes the ball as one that “takes the sway out of the floors around it”. So it never claims that this damper has stopped earning its keep. The gallery is only the opening scene (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text says that shaped towers “do not drift” and work “unattended and unbilled”, so shaping can sound like the better choice.
distractors.why_wrong: The text refuses to rank them: “Neither is obviously the safer bet” (step 3). A shape can also lose part of its benefit for good when a new building goes up upwind, as at the Halberd, where the rise in sway “has not gone away”.

distractors.why_tempting: Safety margins for wind are a familiar topic in discussions of tall buildings.
distractors.why_wrong: The text is about the sway that people feel, measured with accelerometers and checked against complaint logs. It never mentions wind loads or design margins.

p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “mainly about” questions, look for a summing-up sentence – here the one that begins “So” in the last paragraph – and choose the option that states the same contrast.
p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: The vivid opening scene is not the main point. The Verrand’s gallery introduces the subject; the text is about what happens to both methods over the years.

p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The text says that “In eighteen of the nineteen towers the reduction measured in the first year sat within a percentage point or two of what the designers had predicted”. Eighteen of nineteen is all but one. A says this. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the text says about the first year of Rask’s record. The first-year results are in the second paragraph.

steps.title: Find the sentence
steps.text: “In eighteen of the nineteen towers the reduction measured in the first year sat within a percentage point or two of what the designers had predicted, and in the buildings where trouble had been expected — the slender ones, on exposed corners — the complaints did not arrive.”

steps.title: Put it in plain words
steps.text: Eighteen of nineteen means all but one, and within a percentage point or two means very close to the prediction. The text sums up: “The dampers work, and they work about as well as the brochures say.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A restates the result. B says that the slender towers gained little, but there “the complaints did not arrive”; C moves a later problem into the first year; and D invents trials that the text never mentions.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: In all but one tower, the first-year reduction was close to the prediction. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: B sounds careful, and it picks up the slender towers on exposed corners from the text.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite about those towers: they were where trouble had been expected, and “the complaints did not arrive” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text does say that the link between a damper and its tower’s frequency matters, so C sounds connected.
distractors.why_wrong: The drift is a later development: the text gives the frequency for year ten and the fall in benefit by year eight. In the first year, eighteen of the nineteen towers came within a point or two of the prediction (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Testing each damper before certifying it sounds like careful, proper method.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says that Rask’s group samples “continuously rather than in the week of handover tests”. It never mentions forced-vibration trials or any certifying.

p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: When a question names a time – here the first year – find the sentence about that time and keep it apart from later results. Then check the numbers: “eighteen of the nineteen” is “all but one”.
p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: The cautious-sounding option is not always right. Here the text gives a strong, clear result, and B’s caution about the slender towers contradicts it.

p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The text says that “every addition of mass drags the frequency down”: partitions, paper, machinery and water all add mass. By year ten the frequency sat on average about four percent below the damper’s setting. D says this. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what happened to the towers’ natural frequencies over the twelve years. A tower’s natural frequency is the rate at which it sways back and forth on its own, and a damper is set against it.

steps.title: Find the cause
steps.text: “Fit-out adds partitions, tenants add paper and machinery, mechanical rooms take on water, and every addition of mass drags the frequency down.” Fit-out is the work of fitting the inside of a building with walls, furniture and equipment.

steps.title: Find the size
steps.text: “Across the nineteen towers the frequency measured in year ten sat on average some four percent below the value the damper had been set against, and in the three most heavily fitted-out buildings nearer seven.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D gives both the direction and the cause. A has the frequency rising, B says that it held steady, and C takes the figure for the three most fitted-out towers, “nearer seven”, and makes it a full seven percent for every tower.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The frequencies fell as the buildings took on mass. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: A uses the text’s details about fit-out, and stiffening a building can sound like something fit-out would do.
distractors.why_wrong: The text gives the opposite direction: every addition of mass “drags the frequency down” (step 2). It says nothing about stiffening.

distractors.why_tempting: Wear in moving parts is the usual reason a machine loses its effect over time.
distractors.why_wrong: The text rules this out: the benefit fell “not because anything had broken, but because the building had walked away from its own damper”. The frequencies did not hold; they fell (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Seven percent is a figure from the text.
distractors.why_wrong: The figure was “nearer seven” only in “the three most heavily fitted-out buildings”. The average across all nineteen was about four percent (step 3).

p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a question asks how something changed, check both the direction (up or down) and the size, and see whether a figure applies to every case or only to some.
p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: An extreme figure from a few cases can be passed off as the general result. “Nearer seven” applies to three towers, not to all nineteen.

p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: A shape is designed for the wind as it arrives, and a new building upwind changes that wind: after a block went up near the Halberd, the tower’s crosswind sway rose and has stayed higher. So how well a shape works depends partly on buildings that did not exist when it was designed. C says this. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Suggest” means that the answer is not stated outright. Start from Rask’s remark that a shape is tuned “Not to a frequency — to a wind” and work out what follows.

steps.title: Find what a shape is tuned to
steps.text: “The modeling assumes the directions the wind arrives from and the ground it crosses on the way in”. So a shape is designed for the wind as it reaches the site.

steps.title: Find the example
steps.text: “when a forty-story block went up two hundred meters upwind of the Halberd, the accelerometers there recorded a rise in crosswind response that has not gone away. Nobody can notch the Halberd now.” A new building changed the wind reaching the Halberd, and the tower’s shape could not be changed to match.

steps.title: Draw the inference
steps.text: So part of what a shape is worth is decided by buildings put up later – buildings its designers could not see. Rask thinks that an honest comparison would have to name “the blocks not yet built”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C states this. A blames the Halberd’s designers, although the text puts the change down to a later block; B says that shapes can be retuned, although “Nobody can notch the Halberd now”; and D gives planning advice that the text never offers.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: A shaped tower’s worth depends partly on buildings that come later. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: Its first half is true: the modelling does assume wind directions, and the Halberd is the text’s example.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says that the Halberd’s designers chose the wrong directions. The rise in sway came after a new block went up upwind (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Rask’s word “tuned” makes a shape sound like a damper, which can be retuned.
distractors.why_wrong: The text stresses the opposite: a retuned damper got almost all its benefit back, but “Nobody can notch the Halberd now” (step 3). A shape’s advantage cannot be restored, so B misses the real difference.

distractors.why_tempting: If new buildings upwind can harm a shaped tower, keeping the area around it low sounds like a sensible precaution.
distractors.why_wrong: The text gives no such advice. It describes what one new block did to the Halberd, and Rask “will not tell an owner which to build”.

p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: When a question asks what the text suggests follows from an idea, take the stated idea – here a shape is tuned to a wind – and join it to the example the text gives. The right answer is the one-step consequence, not blame or advice that the text never offers.
p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Do not add blame or advice. The Halberd example shows that later buildings matter; it does not say that anyone made a mistake or what should be done.

p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The writer accepts Marek’s point that a shape keeps working: shaped towers “do not drift” and work “for as long as the building stands”. But the writer concludes: “Neither is obviously the safer bet.” That is A. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s attitude to Marek’s case. Keep the voices apart: Marek, Rask and the writer.

steps.title: Find Marek’s case
steps.text: Marek says: “A damper is a maintenance contract you have signed on behalf of everyone who owns the building after you” and “A shape is a decision made once. One of those survives a change of owner. The other does not.”

steps.title: Find what the writer grants
steps.text: The writer agrees that shapes last: “Towers that manage the wind by their shape do not drift”, and they go on breaking up the vortex shedding – the regular peeling-away of air that pushes a tower sideways – “for as long as the building stands, unattended and unbilled”.

steps.title: Find what the writer denies
steps.text: But a shape can be weakened by a new building upwind, as at the Halberd, and it cannot be put right. The writer concludes: “So the damper's advantage decays and can be restored; the shape's advantage does not decay and cannot be. Neither is obviously the safer bet”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches: the writer grants that a shape lasts but denies that this makes it the safer choice. B treats the Halberd as a minor exception, C gives Marek’s view to the writer, and D calls Marek’s view vanity, which the text never does.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer grants Marek’s point about lasting, but not that this makes a shape the safer choice. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: B sounds measured, and the Brayle record does show dampers losing much of their benefit – by year eight the median tower got “rather less than half” of it – which seems to support Marek.
distractors.why_wrong: The Halberd is not a minor exception: it shows that a shape’s advantage can be weakened and “cannot be” restored. The writer’s verdict is that “Neither is obviously the safer bet” (step 4), which does not bear Marek out.

distractors.why_tempting: Marek’s line “A shape is a decision made once” is the most memorable in the text.
distractors.why_wrong: That is Marek’s view, put “without qualification”, that is, with no reservations. The writer does not share it: “Neither is obviously the safer bet” (step 4).

distractors.why_tempting: The writer does push back against Marek’s case, so a sharply negative option can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never calls Marek’s view vanity, and the writer grants that shaped towers “do not drift” (step 3). The writer only denies that shaping is obviously the safer choice.

p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For attitude questions, look for what the writer grants and what the writer denies. A concession – here that shapes do not drift – does not mean that the writer accepts the whole case.
p5-elf-b10-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Do not take the most quotable voice for the writer’s. Marek speaks “without qualification”, that is, with no reservations; the writer weighs both sides.

p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: A screen is “an expensive box to keep warm”, so the gap needs the regular running costs of a business. Those are its overheads, and money that pays for them “covers the overheads”. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “a screen is an expensive box to keep warm, so what stays behind rarely covers the ___”. What stays behind is the share of the ticket money that the cinema keeps: Meng reckons that in a film’s opening week “rather more than half goes back to the distributor”.

steps.title: Find the noun
steps.text: Overheads are the regular costs of running a business, such as heating, rent and staff. “An expensive box to keep warm” points to exactly such costs, and “covers the overheads” is a common way to say that income pays for them.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: All four options begin with over-. “Overtures” are opening moves or the music at the start of an opera, “overhangs” are parts that stick out over something, and “overspills” are what flows over the edge. None of them is a cost that income has to cover.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Rarely covers the overheads” is the only natural reading. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: “Overtures” belongs to the world of entertainment, since an opera or a show can open with an overture.
distractors.why_wrong: An overture is an opening piece of music or a first friendly approach to someone. It is not a cost, and income does not cover overtures (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A cinema is a building, and an overhang is part of a building.
distractors.why_wrong: An overhang is a part that sticks out, such as the edge of a roof. The sentence is about the costs that the cinema’s share of the ticket money rarely covers, and an overhang is not a running cost (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Overspills” suggests something left over, and the sentence is about the money that stays behind.
distractors.why_wrong: An overspill is what spills over the edge, such as water from a full container. The gap needs the costs that the money must pay for (step 2).

p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a gap follows a verb such as “covers”, ask what that verb normally takes when money is involved. Income covers costs, and the regular costs of a business are its overheads.
p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: All four options start with over-, so the look of the word gives nothing away. Use the money context – the box office and the distributor – to choose.

p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The sentence before says that what the cinema keeps of the ticket money rarely covers the overheads. The gapped sentence gives the result: “the counter is where the margin lives”. A connective for a result is “Consequently”. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens “___, the counter is where the margin lives.” The sentence before ends: “so what stays behind rarely covers the overheads”. The margin is the difference between what something costs and what it sells for.

steps.title: Find the relationship
steps.text: If the cinema’s share of the ticket money rarely covers the costs, the profit must come from somewhere else: the counter. So the gapped sentence states a result of the one before, and the figures that follow back it up: figures Meng gathered from four independent sites in 2024 put the gross margin on a tub of popcorn “between eighty and ninety per cent”. “Consequently” means as a result.

steps.title: Check the other connectives
steps.text: “Incidentally” introduces a side remark, “Ostensibly” means apparently but perhaps not really, and “Historically” means in the past or by long tradition. None of them fits: the gapped sentence is the main point of the paragraph, it is presented as true, and it follows as a result from the sentence before.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Consequently, the counter is where the margin lives” follows from the costs. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: “Incidentally” is a common way to start a new point.
distractors.why_wrong: “Incidentally” marks a passing remark. This sentence is the main claim of the paragraph, and the figures after it support it (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Ostensibly” sounds clever and formal, and claims about money are often doubted.
distractors.why_wrong: “Ostensibly” means that something only seems true. The text backs the claim with Meng’s figures – a gross margin of eighty to ninety per cent on a tub of popcorn – so it is presented as really true (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Cinemas have sold popcorn for a long time, so a word about the past can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: “Historically” would make the sentence about the past or about a long tradition, and it gives no link to the sentence before. But this sentence is a result of that one: the cinema’s share of the ticket money rarely covers the overheads, so the margin has to come from the counter (step 2).

p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: For a connective gap, ask how the gapped sentence relates to the one before. When the earlier sentence names a problem and the gapped one says where the money must come from instead, a result word fits.
p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Formal connectives such as “Ostensibly” sound impressive, but each has a precise meaning. Check that meaning against the sentences on both sides.

p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: “By contrast” sets the ticket against popcorn, whose gross margin in Meng’s figures was eighty to ninety per cent. Once the distributor has been paid, what the cinema keeps of a ticket rarely covers its costs, “however dear it looks at the till”. So the ticket is “a surprisingly unprofitable item”. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “A ticket, by contrast, is a surprisingly ___ item in an exhibitor's accounts once the distributor has been paid, however dear it looks at the till.” An exhibitor is a company that runs cinemas.

steps.title: Use the contrast
steps.text: “By contrast” sets the ticket against the popcorn, whose gross margin in Meng’s figures was “between eighty and ninety per cent”. The words “in an exhibitor's accounts once the distributor has been paid” show that the gap is about what the cinema earns. “Dear” means expensive: the ticket looks expensive to the customer, but once the distributor is paid, what is left rarely even covers the costs. Something that makes no profit is unprofitable.

steps.title: Check the other adjectives
steps.text: “Unaffordable” means too expensive to buy, “unassailable” means impossible to attack or question, and “unrepeatable” means impossible to do again. None of them describes how much a ticket earns the cinema.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “A surprisingly unprofitable item” matches the contrast with the popcorn. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence says that the ticket looks “dear”, which means expensive, so “unaffordable” seems to match.
distractors.why_wrong: Unaffordable is about the buyer. The frame is about “an exhibitor's accounts”, and “however dear it looks at the till” already grants that the ticket seems expensive to the customer (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Unassailable” is a strong, formal word that can sound right in a sentence about business.
distractors.why_wrong: Unassailable means so strong that nobody can attack or question it. A ticket’s place in the accounts is not under attack; the sentence is about how much it earns (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A film’s opening week happens only once, so “unrepeatable” can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: Unrepeatable means impossible to do again. A cinema sells tickets at every screening, so the word makes no sense here, and it says nothing about earnings (step 2).

p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: After “by contrast”, the gap usually names the opposite of what was just described. Here the popcorn earns a lot, so the contrasting word must say that the ticket earns little or nothing.
p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Watch whose point of view the frame takes. The ticket looks dear to the customer, but the gap describes the exhibitor’s accounts.

p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: “Had not risen with them but ___” needs something other than a rise, and the old prices were back by the spring, which fits a fall. To slip is to fall a little. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Takings, when the season's accounts were closed, had not risen with them but ___, and by the spring the old prices were quietly back.” Takings are the money a business takes in.

steps.title: Use “not … but”
steps.text: “Not risen … but ___” means that the gap names something other than a rise. Admissions went up a little, but the money did not follow, and the cinema brought the old prices back – which fits a fall in takings. So the takings slipped.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: “Soared” and “swelled” both mean rose, and rising takings would not fit the old prices coming back by the spring. “Sprouted” is used for plants, hair or new buildings appearing, not for takings.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Had not risen with them but slipped”: the takings fell. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: Admissions rose just before, so a rising verb feels natural.
distractors.why_wrong: Soaring is rising fast. Takings that had soared would not fit what happened next: “by the spring the old prices were quietly back” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text mentions popping maize, so a word for growing plants seems to belong.
distractors.why_wrong: Sprouting is a kind of growing, which the frame rules out with “had not risen”, and “sprouted” is not used for takings (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: “Swelled” is a natural word for money that grows, as when profits swell.
distractors.why_wrong: Swelling is growing, the very thing the frame denies: the takings “had not risen” (step 2).

p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: In a frame like “had not risen … but ___”, the gap says what happened instead, so it cannot mean the same as the word after “not”. Check the sentence for support – here the old prices coming back.
p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: The rise in admissions just before the gap pulls towards a rising verb. Read “had not risen” carefully: the takings did the opposite.

p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: Meng is “less comfortable about where that leaves things”: the customers “least able to walk past a counter” are, as a rule, families with children, and Meng has nothing to offer them “beyond the observation that the alternative is worse”. What Meng lacks is a cure for their problem – a remedy. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Meng has no ___ to offer them beyond the observation that the alternative is worse”. “Them” are the customers “least able to walk past a counter”: as a rule, families “with children in tow”, that is, with children along.

steps.title: Find the noun
steps.text: The paragraph begins: “He is less comfortable about where that leaves things.” Meng sees a problem for these families but cannot solve it; all Meng can offer is the point that things would be worse without the counter. A remedy is a cure or a solution for a problem, so “no remedy to offer them” fits.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: A reminder is something that makes you remember, a remnant is a small piece left over, and a remittance is a payment sent to someone. None of them is a solution to a problem.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “No remedy to offer them”: Meng has no solution for these families. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: “Reminder” looks like “remedy”, and Meng does point something out to the families.
distractors.why_wrong: A reminder makes someone remember something. The sentence is about a problem Meng cannot solve, and what is missing is a solution, not a reminder (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Remnant” shares the rem- start and sounds like something that could be handed over.
distractors.why_wrong: A remnant is a small piece left over, such as a bit of cloth. It is not something you offer people as help with a problem (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text is about money, and a remittance is a payment.
distractors.why_wrong: A remittance is money sent to someone. The frame says that the observation is the only ___ Meng can offer: “no ___ to offer them beyond the observation”. An observation can be a kind of answer to a problem, but it cannot be a payment (step 2).

p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: When a gap names what someone lacks, read the sentences before it for the problem. A missing solution to a problem is a remedy.
p5-elf-b10-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: All four options begin with rem-, so they look alike. Decide what Meng lacks – a solution – before choosing the word.
